# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XX. GRACE MAKES A FRIEND

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

At school the following day, Grace faced a difficult time. The story regarding Adam had been spread by Mary Stubbs, leading every scholar, with the exception of the Carrows, to view the matter as entirely humorous. Amidst giggles, the girls informed Grace that the situation was indeed unfortunate, while sarcastic messages of sympathy were written to her by the boys. Grace returned home from school in a miserable state, experiencing a deep sense of internal soreness and pain.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0000 }

“I am heading across to Hollowmere so I can speak with Mrs. Carrow,” she wept. “Unlike all the others, she will not mock me. I simply must speak to someone who comprehends the depth of my distress.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0001 }

She made her way down through Fern Hollow. Magic had been active during the previous night. A dusting of snow had come down, and the powdered firs were imagining an approaching spring and a future delight. The extended hill farther away was deeply purple from leafless beeches. The pinkish glow of sunset rested upon the earth like a rose-colored kiss. Among all the delicate, magical spots, brimming with strange, fairy-like elegance, Fern Hollow on that winter evening was the loveliest. However, its entire dreamlike beauty was unappreciated by poor, heartbroken little Grace.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0002 }

Beside the stream she unexpectedly met Clementine Ainslie, who occupied the old pine tree. Home was her destination after leaving Hollowmere, the place where she had just provided the music lesson to the girls. A fair amount of time had passed while she tarried in Fern Hollow, gazing over its pale loveliness and wandering down several paths of reverie. To judge by her facial expression, her reflections were agreeable. It was possible that the gentle, sporadic clinking of the bells on the Tree Lovers produced the subtle, hidden smile upon her mouth. Alternatively, it might have been created by the awareness that John Ashdown rarely missed spending Monday evening at the gray house situated on the white, wind-blown hill.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0003 }

Grace Ashdown, overflowing with defiant resentment, rushed into Clementine’s dreams. Upon noticing Miss Ainslie, Grace came to a sudden halt. Her acquaintance with her was minimal—only sufficient to exchange greetings upon meeting. Furthermore, she wished to avoid everyone at that moment—save for Mrs. Carrow. Aware that her nose and eyes were crimson and puffy, she despised the thought of a unfamiliar person discovering she had wept.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0004 }

“Good evening, Miss Ainslie,” she uttered, feeling ill at ease.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0005 }

In a gentle tone, Clementine inquired, “What is the matter, Grace?”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0006 }

“Nothing,” Grace replied, speaking somewhat abruptly.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0007 }

“Ah!” Clementine gave a smile. “It is your inability to share anything with those from the outside that you are referring to, isn't it?”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0008 }

A sudden interest stirred in Grace as she looked at Miss Ainslie. This individual possessed a true understanding of things. Furthermore, her beauty was striking! Beneath her plumy hat, her hair shone with such gold! Above her velvet coat, her cheeks showed such pinkness! Her eyes appeared so blue and friendly! It seemed to Grace that a lovely friend could be found in Miss Ainslie—if she were merely a friend rather than a stranger!
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0009 }

“I—I am heading upstairs to inform Mrs. Carrow,” Grace declared. “Her understanding is constant—we are never mocked by her. I habituate discussing matters with her. Assistance comes from it.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0010 }

“My dear girl, it grieves me to inform you that Mrs. Carrow is away,” Miss Ainslie remarked with sympathy. “Having departed for Brierley today, she will remain absent until the week ends.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0011 }

The lip of Grace trembled.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0012 }

“In that case, I may as well return home,” she stated with sorrow.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0013 }

“I believe that is true—unless you feel able to discuss it with me instead,” Miss Clementine offered softly. “Discussing things provides so much relief. I am aware of that. I doubt I am capable of understanding as well as Mrs. Carrow—yet I assure you I will not laugh.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0014 }

“You wouldn’t laugh on the exterior,” Grace demurred. “However, you could—within.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0015 }

“Neither would I chuckle internally. For what reason would I? You have been harmed by something—witnessing anyone in pain is never entertaining to me, regardless of the cause of their distress. Should you experience a desire to inform me about what has caused your pain, I will gladly pay attention. However, if you believe you would prefer to keep it to yourself—that is completely fine as well, my darling.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0016 }

Grace gazed once more into the eyes of Miss Ainslie with a prolonged, sincere look. They appeared deeply earnest, containing not a trace of mirth, even in their furthest depths. Letting out a quiet sigh, she seated herself on the ancient pine near her recently made companion and recounted the entire story of Adam along with his harsh destiny.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0017 }

Laughter was far from Clementine, nor did she have any inclination toward it. Comprehension and empathy filled her—in truth, her capacity nearly matched that of Mrs. Carrow—indeed, it fully equaled hers.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0018 }

“Although Mr. Perry serves as a minister, he ought to have worked as a butcher,” Grace remarked with bitterness. “Carving things up brings him so much pleasure. Taking poor Adam apart gave him genuine enjoyment. He simply carved into him precisely like he was some ordinary rooster.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0019 }

“Giggling slightly—though Grace realized this was directed at Mr. Perry rather than Adam—Clementine remarked, “Grace, speaking privately, I do not care much for Mr. Perry either.” “He was never a favorite of mine. My school days were spent alongside him—as you are aware, he hailed from Glen—and in those days he was an utterly insufferable young prig. My goodness, the female students thoroughly despised grasping his chubby, damp palms during ring-around games. Nevertheless, my dear, we ought to keep in mind that he was unaware Adam held special status as your cherished companion. He assumed the bird was merely an ordinary rooster. Even amidst immense grief, fairness is required of us.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0020 }

“I guess that’s true,” Grace conceded. “However, Miss Ainslie, why is it that everyone appears to find my great love for Adam so humorous? No one would have found it odd if the pet had been a miserable old cat. Everyone felt sympathy for Lottie Warren when the binder severed her kitten’s legs. She wept in school for two days without anyone mocking her, not even Dan Coyle. Furthermore, all her close friends attended the kitten’s burial service and assisted her in interring it—except they were unable to inter its unfortunate small paws alongside it, since they were impossible to locate. Naturally, that was a terrible event to occur, but to my mind it was not as horrific as witnessing your pet being devoured. Still, everyone makes fun of me.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0021 }

“My belief is that it stems from the word ‘rooster’ sounding somewhat amusing,” Clementine stated seriously. “A humorous quality exists within it. Conversely, ‘chicken’ is not the same. Speaking about being fond of a chicken does not strike one as nearly so amusing.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0022 }

“Adam was the sweetest tiny chick, Miss Ainslie. He was merely a small ball of gold. He used to rush toward me to eat from my hand. Furthermore, he was good-looking when he matured, as well—pure white, boasting a lovely, curved white tail, even if Mary Stubbs claimed it lacked length. He recognized his name and consistently appeared whenever I summoned him—he was an exceptionally smart rooster. Moreover, Aunt Martha possessed no right to slaughter him. He belonged to me. It was not just, was it, Miss Ainslie?”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0023 }

“No, it was not,” Clementine stated with conviction. “It was not fair at all. I recall owning a pet hen during my childhood. That creature was extremely pretty—completely golden brown with small spots. My love for her matched the affection I ever felt for any animal companion. Her life was not ended by slaughter—she passed away from advanced years. Mother refused to permit her to be slaughtered owing to her being my pet.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0024 }

“Had my mother still been alive, Adam’s death would not have been allowed by her,” Grace remarked. “And as for father, he would not have permitted it either, had he been back and aware of the situation. Of that I am certain, Miss Ainslie.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0025 }

“I’m positive, as well,” stated Clementine. Her cheeks displayed a slight extra color. She appeared somewhat self-aware, yet Grace failed to observe any of it.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0026 }

“Did I act very wrongly by keeping quiet about Mr. Perry’s coat-tails burning?” she inquired with concern.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0027 }

“Oh, terribly wicked,” replied Clementine, her eyes dancing. “However, I would have behaved just as badly, Grace—I wouldn’t have informed him that they were burning—and I do not think I would have ever felt the slightest remorse for my bad behavior, either.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0028 }

“Ida was of the opinion that I ought to have informed him on the grounds that he was a clergyman.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0029 }

“My dear, should a minister fail to act like a gentleman, we have no obligation to honor his coat-tails. I am certain I would have simply adored watching Jimmy Perry’s coat-tails catch fire. That had to be entertaining.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0030 }

A laugh came from both of them, though a faint, resentful sigh marked the end of Grace's.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0031 }

“Well, regardless, Adam has passed away and I will not love anything ever again.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0032 }

“Avoid speaking like that, my dear. If we fail to love, we forfeit a great deal of life's value. Life grows wealthier in proportion to how much we love—even when the object is merely a tiny pet with fur or feathers. Is a canary something you would want, Grace—a small, golden creature of a canary? Should you desire it, I will present you with one. Up at our home, there are two.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0033 }

“Oh, I would like that,” Grace exclaimed. “Birds are a favorite of mine. Only—would Aunt Martha’s cat consume it? Having your pets consumed is extremely tragic. I doubt I could bear it once more.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0034 }

“Should you suspend the cage a sufficient distance from the wall, it seems unlikely to me that the cat would be able to hurt it. I am going to explain to you precisely how you ought to attend to it, and I am going to convey it to Hollowmere on your behalf the very next time I travel down.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0035 }

Clementine was reflecting within her own mind,
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0036 }

“Every local busybody in the Glen will be provided with a topic of conversation by this, yet I shall be indifferent. I wish to bring solace to this unfortunate small heart.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0037 }

Grace found solace in these moments, finding the sympathy and understanding to be deeply comforting. Alongside Miss Clementine, she remained seated on the old pine as dusk gently descended across the white valley and the evening star began to glow above the gray maple grove. Grace shared her entire modest past and aspirations with Clementine, detailing her preferences and aversion, the intricacies of living at the manse, as well as the fluctuations of school life. Ultimately, when they separated, a strong friendship had been established.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0038 }

When the evening meal commenced, Mr. Ashdown was absorbed in his typical reveries, yet before long, a specific name penetrated his daydreaming and restored his attention to the present. Grace was recounting to Ida how she had encountered Clementine.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0039 }

“In my opinion, she is simply delightful,” Grace remarked. “Equally pleasant as Mrs. Carrow—though in another way. It made me want to embrace her. She actually embraced me—a wonderfully soft, velvety embrace. On top of that, she addressed me as ‘dearest.’ It gave me a wonderful thrill. I felt capable of confiding anything to her.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0040 }

“So Miss Ainslie met with your approval, Grace?” inquired Mr. Ashdown, using a somewhat strange tone.
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0041 }

“Grace cried, “I love her.”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0042 }

“Ah!” Mr. Ashdown said. “Ah!”
{: #nw-v05-c20-p0043 }
